intro: You've searched for a lawyer, which usually means something in your life has reached a point where legal advice would help — a contract, a dispute, a family matter, a property move or a problem at work. The word covers a range of roles, so the first useful step is working out which kind of legal professional you actually need. We introduce people to UK solicitors who can quote you directly for the work.
need_heading: What people searching for a lawyer usually need
need_lead: A lawyer can help you understand your position, prepare documents, negotiate on your behalf and, where necessary, run a court case.
needs: You're buying or selling a home and need someone to handle the conveyancing and check the title.
You're going through a separation or divorce and need advice on finances, children or a settlement.
You've received a letter before claim or a court form and need to know how to respond.
You're starting or running a business and need help with a contract, a lease or a dispute.
You're dealing with a probate or estate administration matter and need guidance on the legal steps.
context_heading: One key thing to understand when searching for a lawyer
context: The word "lawyer" is not protected on its own, so it is worth checking that whoever handles your matter is a solicitor, a chartered legal executive or another authorised professional. Reserved activities such as conducting court litigation and certain probate and conveyancing work can only be carried out by authorised people.

Solicitors in England and Wales are regulated by the Solicitors Regulation Authority, and you can check an individual or firm on the SRA's register. In Scotland solicitors are regulated by the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland by the Law Society of Northern Ireland. Regulated firms must hold professional indemnity insurance and have a complaints procedure.
tell_heading: What to tell iComply when you enquire
tell: Describe the legal matter in a sentence or two, such as a house purchase, a family issue or a business contract.
Say where you are in the UK, because the legal system and the regulator differ between England and Wales, Scotland and Northern Ireland.
Mention whether any deadline or court date is coming up, so the solicitor can prioritise.
Explain whether you have already received legal letters or court papers about the matter.
Say whether you are looking for one-off advice, help with documents, or full representation.
Include any preference for how you would like to communicate, such as by phone, email or in person.
questions: Are you regulated by the SRA, the Law Society of Scotland or the Law Society of Northern Ireland, and can you give me your registration number?
Do you specialise in the type of matter I've described, and how often do you handle cases like mine?
What are your fees and how will you keep me informed about costs as the matter progresses?
Who will actually be handling my matter day to day, and are they a solicitor or another authorised professional?
What are the likely timescales and what do you need from me to get started?
What is your complaints procedure if I am unhappy with the service?

faqs.q: How do I check that a lawyer is properly regulated?
faqs.a: For solicitors in England and Wales, you can search the SRA's register online. In Scotland, check with the Law Society of Scotland, and in Northern Ireland with the Law Society of Northern Ireland. This confirms whether the individual or firm is authorised to practise.

faqs.q: What is the difference between a solicitor and a barrister?
faqs.a: A solicitor usually handles the day-to-day legal work, gives advice, prepares documents and negotiates for you. A barrister is a specialist advocate, often instructed by a solicitor to represent you in court. For many matters, your first point of contact will be a solicitor.

faqs.q: Will I be told how much the legal work will cost?
faqs.a: Regulated firms are expected to give you information about costs at the start, and you can ask for an estimate or a fixed fee where possible. Costs can change if the matter becomes more complex, so ask how you will be updated. iComply does not set or quote fees; the solicitor quotes you directly.

faqs.q: Can I complain if I am unhappy with the service?
faqs.a: Regulated firms must have a complaints procedure, and you should ask for a copy. If the complaint is not resolved, in England and Wales you can take service complaints to the Legal Ombudsman. In Scotland and Northern Ireland, the relevant professional body can advise on the route.

extra_heading: Working out which kind of lawyer your matter needs
extra: Searching simply for a lawyer tells us you may not yet know whether your matter belongs with a solicitor, a chartered legal executive or another authorised professional. Legal work is divided into specialisms, so a conveyancing matter, a family separation and a business dispute will usually be handled by different people with different experience. Naming the area of law in your own words is often more useful than picking a job title.

It also helps to think about what you actually want from the person you instruct. Some people need a one-off piece of advice or a document reviewed, while others need someone to negotiate on their behalf or represent them in court. Being clear about that from the start means the professional you speak to can tell you honestly whether the work sits within their expertise.

Finally, remember that the legal system differs across the UK, so where you live affects which regulator applies and which courts or procedures are involved. Mentioning your location and the nature of the matter when you contact us lets us introduce you to someone whose work covers that area.

extra_faqs.q: I don't know what area of law my problem falls under — can I still enquire?
extra_faqs.a: Yes. Describe what has happened in plain language, such as a letter you have received, a contract you have signed or a family situation that needs sorting out. We can then introduce you to a solicitor whose work covers that kind of matter, and they can confirm whether they are the right person for it.

extra_faqs.q: Should I speak to a solicitor before I know exactly what I need?
extra_faqs.a: An initial conversation is often the point at which your options become clearer, because a solicitor can explain the legal position and what steps might follow. Ask about costs at that stage so you understand what any further work would involve before you commit.
